content: HIV-infected individuals and AIDS patients often turn to complementary therapies, including herbal medicines, due to dissatisfaction with conventional treatments, which may be associated with limited efficacy, high costs, lack of availability, or adverse effects. The objective of this study was to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of herbal medicines in individuals with HIV infection or AIDS. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, as well as manual searches. The search concluded in December 2004. The study included randomized clinical trials that compared herbal medicines to no intervention, placebo, or antiretroviral drugs in patients with HIV infection, HIV-related diseases, or AIDS. The outcomes assessed included mortality, progression of HIV disease, new AIDS-defining events, CD4 cell counts, viral load, psychological status, quality of life, and adverse effects. Two authors independently extracted data and evaluated the methodological quality of the trials based on criteria such as randomization, allocation concealment, double blinding, and participant drop-out rates. Nine randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving 499 participants with HIV infection or AIDS met the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality was deemed adequate in five trials, while it was unclear in the others. Eight different herbal medicines were tested across these studies. A compound of Chinese herbs known as IGM-1 demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in health-related quality of life in 30 symptomatic HIV-infected patients compared to placebo (weighted mean difference 0.66, 95% confidence interval 0.05 to 1.27). However, IGM-1 did not appear to influence overall health perception, symptom severity, CD4 cell counts, anxiety, or depression. An herbal formulation consisting of 35 Chinese herbs showed no effect on CD4 cell counts, viral load, AIDS-related events, symptoms, psychosocial measures, or quality of life. Additionally, adverse effects were more frequent in the group receiving this herbal preparation (79%) compared to the placebo group (38%) (p = 0.003). The herbal compound SPV30 did not show a statistically significant difference from placebo in terms of new AIDS-defining events, CD4 cell counts, or viral load. However, an earlier pilot study suggested a positive effect of SPV30 on CD4 cell counts. A combination of a Chinese herbal compound (SH) and antiretroviral therapy demonstrated enhanced antiviral benefits compared to antiretroviral therapy alone. The herbal compound SP-303 was found to reduce stool weight (p = 0.008) and abnormal stool frequency (p = 0.04) in 51 AIDS patients with diarrhea. Qiankunning, another herbal medicine, did not affect HIV-1 RNA levels and was associated with side effects such as stomach discomfort and diarrhea. Curcumin was ineffective in reducing viral load or improving CD4 cell counts, and capsaicin did not alleviate pain associated with HIV-related peripheral neuropathy. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of herbal medicines in individuals with HIV infection or AIDS. While some potential benefits were observed, these findings need to be confirmed through larger, more rigorous clinical trials.
